title: A beats B twice. B wins.
blocks: Two treatments for kidney stones. Treatment A beats Treatment B for small stones, and A beats B for large stones. But when you add everyone up, B wins. How is that possible?
Here's the real data from a famous study. For small stones, A cured ninety-three percent of patients and B cured eighty-seven. For large stones, A cured seventy-three percent and B cured sixty-nine.

Now add up everyone. A treated three hundred fifty patients and cured two hundred seventy-three, that's seventy-eight percent. B also treated three hundred fifty and cured two hundred eighty-nine, that's eighty-three percent. B wins overall.

Look at who got what. Treatment A was used mostly on large stones, the hard cases: two hundred sixty-three of its three hundred fifty patients. Treatment B was used mostly on small stones, the easy ones: two hundred seventy of its three hundred fifty.
So A looked worse overall only because it got the hard cases. The groups were not the same size, so the average hid the truth.
Whenever an average hides groups, ask who is in each group. That's Simpson's paradox: the trend can flip when you combine the data.
